n: Elihu begins his fourth and final speech, which builds toward a hymn about God’s power in the storm — preparing the way for God himself to speak.
He asks Job to bear with him a little longer; there is more to say on God’s behalf.

f.g: Be patient with me a bit longer.

n: Elihu will draw on wide-ranging knowledge to show that his Maker is just.
He insists his words are true and boldly calls himself one “perfect in knowledge” — a claim that may sound overconfident, since 37:16 uses the same phrase for God.

f.w: he that is perfect in knowledge

n: God is mighty but does not despise anyone; his strength is matched by his understanding.
He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives justice to the afflicted.
God never takes his eyes off the righteous; he seats them with kings and exalts them forever.

f.w: He withdraweth not his eyes from the righteous
with kings are they on the throne

n: If the righteous find themselves in chains and bound by suffering…

f.g: Ropes of suffering — affliction pictured as bondage.

n: …God uses it to show them what they’ve done and where they’ve proudly overstepped.
He opens their ears to instruction and commands them to turn from wrong.

f.w: openeth also their ear to discipline

n: If they listen and serve him, they will live out their days in prosperity and contentment.

f.w: If they obey and serve him

n: If they refuse, they die by the sword (or “cross the river” of death) without gaining knowledge.
The godless in heart nurse anger instead of crying to God when he disciplines them.

f.g: Store up resentment — or store up God’s wrath for themselves.

n: They die young and in shame, among the male prostitutes of the pagan shrines.

f.g: Hebrew qedeshim — cult prostitutes; an image of a shameful, early death.

n: Elihu’s key insight: God rescues sufferers by means of their suffering and opens their ears through adversity.
God wanted to lure Job out of distress into a wide-open place, with a table full of rich food.

f.w: out of the strait into a broad place

n: But Job is preoccupied with judgment on the wicked, and so judgment and justice grip him.

f.w: fulfilled the judgment of the wicked
f.g: Possibly “you are obsessed with the case against the wicked.”

n: Elihu warns Job not to let anger or riches lure him away, and not to think a large bribe could turn God’s judgment aside.

f.w: a great ransom cannot deliver thee

n: Neither wealth nor strength can help him in distress.
Don’t long for the night of death, when people are swept away.
Beware of turning to evil — Elihu fears Job prefers complaint to patient submission under affliction.
Elihu now turns to God’s greatness: God is exalted in power — who teaches like him?
No one has prescribed God’s ways for him, and no one can rightly say he did wrong.
Remember to praise God’s work, which people have sung about.
Everyone has seen it, even if only from far away.

f.g: Mortals see God’s works only partially, from a distance.

n: God is so great that we cannot fully understand him; his years cannot be counted.
Elihu begins describing the rain cycle: God draws up droplets of water, and they become rain from the mist.

f.w: maketh small the drops of water
f.g: Draws up drops of water — evaporation.

n: The clouds pour it down in showers on people.
Who can understand how clouds spread out, or the thunder that roars from God’s pavilion?

f.g: His canopy or pavilion — the storm clouds.

n: He spreads lightning around himself and covers the depths of the sea.
Through storms God governs the nations — bringing both judgment and abundant food.
He fills his hands with lightning and commands it to strike its target.

f.w: With clouds he covereth the light
f.g: Better “he covers his hands with lightning.”

n: The thunder announces his coming; even the cattle sense the storm approaching. The scene is being set for the whirlwind of chapter 38.

f.w: the cattle also concerning the vapour
f.g: Even livestock sense the coming storm.
